RagShortTexts: In 1214 at Bouvines, Philip II Augustus vanquished an Anglo-Imperial coalition, solidifying.

Variants.Content: On July 27, 1214, Philip II Augustus met a coalition led by Emperor Otto IV and the Count of Flanders near the bridge at Bouvines, on the Flemish border. Communal militias from towns such as Paris and Amiens fought in the ranks beside the feudal knights. Those militias stood firm while the heavy cavalry clashed in close hand-to-hand fighting, and the enemy line broke after the Count of Flanders was taken prisoner. Otto IV fled and lost much of his imperial prestige. The victory strengthened the Capetian crown inside France and made Philip the dominant power in northern Europe. It also left England's king isolated on the continent, where his allies had been captured or humbled.

Bouvines left King John of England weakened abroad, and his barons at home used the failure as proof that his rule had broken down. Their pressure produced Magna Carta at Runnymede in June 1215. For a French town that had sent men to the field, the victory meant its charter was written down and sealed, so the gains of the battle became written rights.
